title: Drought empties Brackmere Reservoir and puts Ardwell Water under investigation
notice: Synthetic text written for this package. The region, the reservoirs, the water company, the regulator, the organisations and the people named here are all invented; this is not a report about any real drought, company or investigation. Written at full newspaper length to exercise the algorithm on realistic long-form input.

documents.text: Brackmere Reservoir fell to 19 percent of capacity on Monday, its lowest level since the drought of 1976, as Ardwell Water confirmed that a hosepipe ban will take effect across the valley from 12 June. The restriction applies to roughly 1.1 million households in Kestrelford and the surrounding towns, and will be followed by a ban on non-essential commercial use if the reservoir falls below 15 percent. Chief executive Rosalind Kerrigan said the company had no realistic alternative after a third consecutive dry winter. Rainfall across the Ardwell catchment has been 42 percent below the long-term average since October, according to figures the company published on Monday morning. The smaller Cold Fell reservoir, which supplies the western half of the valley, stood at 24 percent. Ms Kerrigan said Ardwell Water was not currently planning to introduce standpipes, which have not been used in the region since 1976, but she declined to rule them out for later in the summer. “I am not going to stand here in June and make a promise about September that I cannot keep,” she told reporters at the company's headquarters. The announcement came hours after the national water regulator confirmed that it had opened a formal investigation into the company's leakage record. Ardwell Water lost 22 percent of the water it put into supply to leaks last year, the third-worst performance of any utility in the country. Council leader Priya Nandakumar described that figure as indefensible and called on the regulator to impose a financial penalty. The company has paid out 280 million pounds in dividends over the past five years, while a 340 million pound pipeline intended to link the valley to the neighbouring Wear catchment has been delayed twice. Ms Kerrigan said the pipeline had been held up by planning objections rather than by any shortage of money, and that construction would now begin in the autumn. Farmers on the Lowmoor levels have already had their abstraction licences cut by 30 percent, a restriction the farmers' union estimates will cost the region 70 million pounds in lost crops. Hospitals, schools and care homes are exempt from the hosepipe ban, as are commercial car washes until the second stage of restrictions begins. Households that ignore the ban can be fined up to 1,000 pounds, although Ms Kerrigan said the company had no intention of prosecuting anyone in the first weeks and would rely on what she called neighbourly pressure. The company said it had increased its leak repair crews from 40 to 110 since March and was now fixing about 900 leaks a week. It has also begun tankering water into two villages at the head of the valley where the local supply has already failed. Forecasters expect no significant rainfall in the catchment before the end of the month. The last time Brackmere was this low, in August 1976, the region went 46 days without measurable rain and the army was brought in to distribute water in Kestrelford. Ms Nandakumar said the council had begun contingency planning for standpipes but stressed that no decision had been taken. Falling water levels have exposed the remains of Nether Brack, a village flooded when the reservoir was created in 1954, and the site has drawn several hundred visitors a day. Ardwell Water has asked people to stay away from the exposed shoreline, which it says is unstable. The regulator is expected to report on its investigation in the autumn.

Ardwell Water lost 22 percent of the water it put into supply last year, a rate that has barely improved in a decade and which now sits at the centre of a formal investigation by the national water regulator. The figure equates to about 340 million litres a day disappearing into the ground between the treatment works and the tap, roughly a third of what Brackmere Reservoir still holds. Chief executive Rosalind Kerrigan, who took over in 2021, argues that the company inherited a network of which nearly 40 percent predates the Second World War. “You cannot replace a hundred years of cast iron in three summers,” she said in an interview at the company's Kestrelford headquarters. Critics point out that the company has found money for other things. Ardwell Water has paid 280 million pounds in dividends to its shareholders over the past five years, a period during which capital spending on the network fell in real terms in three of those years. Its debt stands at 1.9 billion pounds, or about 68 percent of the regulatory value of its assets. The 340 million pound pipeline to the Wear catchment, first proposed in 2016 and originally due to be completed in 2023, has been delayed twice and is now scheduled to begin construction in the autumn. Ms Kerrigan attributes both delays to planning objections, particularly from landowners along the eight-mile section that crosses the Lowmoor levels. Documents filed with the regulator in 2019, however, show that the company itself asked for the scheme to be rephased to a later spending period. Analysts at Renner Capital described the company's position as uncomfortable rather than dangerous. “They will be fined, the fine will be affordable, and the political cost will be considerably higher than the financial one,” the firm wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday. The regulator has the power to levy a penalty of up to 10 percent of annual turnover, which in Ardwell Water's case would be about 94 million pounds. It has not imposed a penalty at anything near that level on any company in the past. Ms Kerrigan declined to say whether she would forgo her bonus, which was 410,000 pounds last year on a base salary of 620,000 pounds. She said the question was a matter for the remuneration committee and that she would accept its decision. The company has increased its leak detection teams from 40 to 110 since March, hired 60 additional engineers, and says it is now repairing about 900 leaks a week against a normal summer rate of 300. It has also brought forward the replacement of 14 kilometres of Victorian main in the Northgate district of Kestrelford. Ms Kerrigan said the company would meet its regulatory leakage target for the current five-year period, though she conceded it would do so only in the final year. Shares in the company's listed parent fell 6 percent on Monday and a further 3 percent on Tuesday. The board is due to decide on the interim dividend in September, three weeks before the regulator is expected to publish the findings of its investigation. Several institutional shareholders have privately urged the company to suspend the payout, according to two people familiar with the discussions. Ms Kerrigan would say only that the board was aware of the sensitivities.

Pressure on the national water regulator intensified on Tuesday as members of parliament from across the Ardwell Valley demanded that it impose the largest penalty in its history on Ardwell Water. The regulator confirmed on Monday that it had opened a formal investigation into the company's leakage record, which at 22 percent is the third worst in the country. Fiona Doyle, who represents Kestrelford East, told the Commons that the investigation was welcome but overdue. “This company has been losing a fifth of its water for a decade and the regulator has known it for a decade,” she said. “The question is not what Ardwell Water did wrong this summer. The question is what the regulator did about it in all the summers before.” The regulator's chief executive, Adam Whitcombe, is due to appear before the environment select committee on 26 June. He has previously defended the regulator's record, arguing that leakage across the industry has fallen by 11 percent since 2015 and that the framework rewards long-term investment rather than short-term fixes. Ms Doyle has tabled an amendment that would require water companies to link executive bonuses directly to leakage and pollution performance. The environment secretary said the government was considering the proposal but stopped short of endorsing it. Council leader Priya Nandakumar, who has led the local campaign, said the political response had been too slow. “Every household in this valley is being told to stop watering a garden while the company loses 340 million litres a day into the ground,” she said. “People can do the arithmetic.” The council has begun contingency planning for standpipes in Kestrelford, the first such planning since 1976, and has identified 34 sites where they could be installed. Ms Nandakumar stressed that no decision had been taken and that the planning was precautionary. Opposition members have called for the 340 million pound Wear pipeline to be taken out of the company's hands and delivered by a public body. The environment secretary rejected that suggestion, saying it would delay the scheme by years rather than accelerate it. Ardwell Water has said construction will begin in the autumn, three years later than the original 2023 completion date. Ms Doyle said she would judge the company on whether a spade went into the ground before Christmas. The regulator is expected to report in the autumn, and can levy a penalty of up to 10 percent of annual turnover, about 94 million pounds in Ardwell Water's case. Mr Whitcombe has declined to comment on the likely scale of any fine while the investigation is open. A separate review of the regional drought plan, commissioned by the environment department in March, is due to report in October. Its terms of reference were widened last week to include the question of whether the hosepipe ban should have been imposed in May rather than June. Ms Kerrigan has said the company followed its published drought plan to the letter and that the trigger levels in that plan were approved by the regulator in 2022.

Growers on the Lowmoor levels have had their abstraction licences cut by 30 percent for the rest of the season, a restriction the farmers' union estimates will cost the region 70 million pounds in lost crops. The levels, a 40,000 hectare stretch of drained wetland south of Kestrelford, produce roughly a fifth of the country's salad crop and almost all of its watercress. Tom Sedgwick, who farms 300 hectares of lettuce and celery near Lowmoor St Mary, said he had already ploughed in 18 hectares of crop he could no longer irrigate. “You do not decide to lose a field,” he said. “The field decides, and you watch it decide over about four days.” The abstraction cut applies to water drawn directly from the Ardwell and from the network of drainage channels that criss-cross the levels, both of which are at their lowest recorded levels for June. It does not apply to water taken from on-farm reservoirs, of which there are 61 on the levels, holding between them about 11 days of normal irrigation demand. Mr Sedgwick's reservoir was full in February and is now at a third. The union has asked the environment department for an emergency hardship fund and for the abstraction cut to be reviewed fortnightly rather than monthly. Its regional chairman said the 30 percent figure had been applied uniformly without regard to what each holding actually grows. “A 30 percent cut to a cereal farm in July is an inconvenience,” he said. “A 30 percent cut to a salad grower in July is the whole business.” The department said the restrictions were necessary to protect river flows and the habitats that depend on them, and that it would keep the position under review. Ecologists have warned that flows on the middle Ardwell are approaching the point at which fish kills become likely. The river ran at 0.9 cubic metres a second at the Kestrelford gauge on Monday, against a June average of 4.1. Two tributaries, the Brack and the Sallow, have stopped flowing entirely for the first time since 1976. Farmers have also criticised Ardwell Water's leakage record, arguing that the 22 percent the company loses to leaks would more than cover the water the levels have been told to give up. The company said the comparison was not straightforward because treated water and abstracted river water are not interchangeable. Mr Sedgwick was unimpressed. “It is all the same rain,” he said. Packhouses in Lowmoor have begun taking supply from growers in other regions to keep supermarket contracts intact, which the union says will depress local prices further when the harvest does come. Three growers have told the union they will not plant a second crop this season. The levels employ about 4,200 people directly, a figure that rises to 9,000 during the harvest, and the union has warned that seasonal recruitment for August is already down by a third. The county council has convened a drought group that will meet weekly through the summer. Its first meeting on Wednesday was told that the levels would need 120 millimetres of rain in the next six weeks to avoid what one official described as a structural loss to the sector. The forecast for the next fortnight is dry.

The drought now emptying Brackmere Reservoir began in October 2022, and understanding why it has been so severe means looking below the ground rather than above it. Rainfall across the Ardwell catchment has been 42 percent below the long-term average since October, which is exceptional but not unprecedented. What makes this year different is that it is the third consecutive dry winter, and winter is when the aquifer beneath the valley is supposed to refill. “In a normal year the chalk recharges between November and March, and that stored water is what keeps the rivers running in August,” said Dr Owen Blake, a hydrologist at the University of Kestrelford. “We have now missed three recharge seasons in a row. The reservoir is the visible problem. The aquifer is the real one.” Groundwater levels at the Cold Fell monitoring borehole are the lowest recorded since measurements began there in 1958. Dr Blake said the aquifer would need two consecutive wet winters to return to normal, and that a single wet autumn would refill the reservoirs while leaving the underlying deficit largely intact. That distinction matters for how long restrictions last. Brackmere can refill in about eleven weeks of sustained rainfall; the aquifer takes years. The 1976 drought, which is the comparison everyone in the valley reaches for, followed a similar pattern of consecutive dry winters, but it broke in a single extraordinary September. Dr Blake cautioned against expecting a repeat. “1976 ended because the weather did something unusual, not because anybody managed it well,” he said. Climate projections for the region suggest that summers will be drier and winters wetter by mid-century, which sounds neutral but is not. Wetter winters deliver more of their rain in intense bursts that run off the surface rather than soaking in, so the aquifer sees less benefit than the total suggests. Dr Blake's group modelled the catchment under three scenarios last year and found that the frequency of a Brackmere-level drought roughly triples by 2060 without additional storage or transfer capacity. That finding was cited by Ardwell Water in support of its 340 million pound Wear pipeline, though Dr Blake noted that his team had also modelled demand reduction and leakage repair, which delivered a comparable benefit at lower cost. “A pipeline moves the problem to a different catchment,” he said. “Fixing 22 percent leakage removes it.” River flows are already at levels that threaten aquatic life. The Ardwell ran at 0.9 cubic metres a second at the Kestrelford gauge on Monday against a June average of 4.1, and two tributaries have stopped flowing entirely. Water temperatures in the remaining pools reached 24 degrees last week, close to the limit for brown trout. The environment department has begun rescuing fish from isolated pools on the Brack, an operation last mounted in the valley in 2018. Dr Blake said the exposure of Nether Brack, the village flooded in 1954 and now visible above the waterline at Brackmere, was a useful public reminder but a poor scientific indicator. The village last appeared in 1976, 1995 and 2011, and its reappearance says only that the reservoir is low, which everybody already knows. What would tell you more, he said, is the borehole record, and almost nobody reads it.

For nine weeks the village of Nether Brack has been standing in the sun for the first time in fourteen years, and about four hundred people a day have been walking down the cracked mud of the Brackmere shoreline to look at it. There is not a great deal to see: the footings of some thirty houses, a packhorse bridge with both parapets gone, the stump of a church tower, and a line of stones that was once the road to Kestrelford. It is enough. Nether Brack was flooded in 1954 when the valley was dammed to supply a city that had doubled in size in thirty years. Its 214 residents were moved to a new estate on the northern edge of Kestrelford, where the streets were named after the lanes they had left. Eleven of those residents are still alive. Margaret Aylward, who is 81 and was nine when her family left, has been down to the shoreline three times this summer. “The first time I could not find the house,” she said. “The second time I realised I had been standing on it.” She remembers the water coming up slowly over two winters, and her father refusing to watch. The village has emerged four times since: in 1976, 1995, 2011 and now. Each appearance has been shorter and, in the way of these things, better attended. In 1976 a local photographer took eleven pictures over three days; this summer the site appeared on social media within hours and the car park at Fell Gate was full by nine in the morning for a fortnight. Ardwell Water has asked people to stay off the exposed bed, which it describes as unstable, and has put up rope and eight signs. Both are widely ignored. The county archaeologist, who has been recording the site since the water dropped below the church, said the exposure was scientifically valuable and physically dangerous in roughly equal measure. Two people have been treated for injuries after sinking to the thigh in silt near the old mill. “The mud looks like a beach and behaves like a bog,” she said. What the exposure has also done is reopen an argument that the valley has never quite finished. The reservoir was built by compulsory purchase against a campaign that lasted six years, and the compensation paid to the tenant farmers of Nether Brack was, by the standards of the time, ungenerous. A group of descendants has spent the summer lobbying for a permanent memorial on the shore, and the county council agreed in principle last week. Ms Aylward is unsentimental about it. “They needed the water,” she said. “Kestrelford was drinking out of the Ardwell and the Ardwell was filthy. I have never met anyone from the village who thought the reservoir was wrong. We thought the money was wrong.” She has watched the coverage of the hosepipe ban with a certain grim amusement. Her own garden, she said, has not been watered since May and looks no worse than her neighbour's. When the rain comes, the water will rise over Nether Brack again, probably within a season. Ms Aylward said she expected to see it once more. “I saw it in 1976 and I thought that was the last time,” she said. “Then 1995, and I thought that was the last time.”

The hosepipe ban that took effect across the Ardwell Valley on 12 June is the visible part of a set of restrictions that will cost the regional economy considerably more than the inconvenience to gardeners suggests. Business groups put the immediate cost at between 180 and 240 million pounds, most of it concentrated in agriculture, food processing and tourism. The largest single component is the 70 million pounds the farmers' union expects the Lowmoor levels to lose after abstraction licences were cut by 30 percent. Behind that sit the packhouses, hauliers and seasonal labour contractors that depend on the harvest. Three of the valley's four salad packhouses have begun buying in produce from other regions to hold their supermarket contracts, which protects the contract and undercuts the local grower simultaneously. The Kestrelford brewery, the largest industrial water user in the valley outside the food sector, has cut production by 15 percent and brought forward its annual maintenance shutdown to July. Its managing director said the decision was voluntary and pre-emptive. “If we are going to be told to stop in August, I would rather choose to slow down in July,” he said. Commercial car washes, of which there are 94 in the valley, are exempt from the current restriction but would be closed by the second stage, which triggers if Brackmere falls below 15 percent. The reservoir stood at 19 percent on Monday. The tourism position is more mixed than the headlines suggest. Bookings at the four large caravan parks around the reservoir are up 9 percent on last year, driven largely by visitors coming to see the exposed remains of Nether Brack. Hotels in Kestrelford report a smaller rise. Against that, the two golf courses on the northern shore have closed their watered greens, three canoe operators have suspended trading because the launch ramps now end in mud, and the reservoir's own visitor centre has cut its opening hours because it cannot fill its water tanks. The regional chamber of commerce has asked the government for a hardship scheme along the lines of the one offered during the 2018 drought, and for business rates relief for firms that can demonstrate a supply-driven loss of trade. The environment department said it was monitoring the position. Ardwell Water has set up a commercial liaison line and says it has agreed individual supply arrangements with 41 large users. It has resisted calls to compensate businesses affected by restrictions, pointing out that its licence obliges it to protect essential supply first. That argument has not gone down well alongside the 280 million pounds the company has paid in dividends over the past five years, or its 22 percent leakage rate. The chamber's chief executive was blunt. “Our members are being asked to absorb a loss caused by an infrastructure failure they did not cause and cannot fix,” she said. Analysts caution that the headline cost figures are soft. Much of the lost salad crop will be replaced by production elsewhere in the country, so the national figure is far smaller than the regional one, and some of the tourism loss is offset by the reservoir's own grim novelty. The durable damage, they argue, is to investment confidence. Two food processing firms that had been considering expansion in the valley have paused their decisions pending clarity on long-term water availability. Both cited the repeated delays to the 340 million pound Wear pipeline rather than the drought itself.

Everyone in the Ardwell Valley is talking about 1976, and almost everyone is drawing the wrong lesson from it. The comparison is irresistible: Brackmere Reservoir at 19 percent, the lowest since that summer, standpipes being discussed for the first time in half a century, and the drowned village of Nether Brack up out of the water again as though on cue. But 1976 was a weather event that ended when the weather changed. What the valley faces now is a weather event landing on top of an infrastructure decision, and only one of those two things was ever within anybody's control. Consider what has and has not been built. In 1976 the valley was served by two reservoirs and an aquifer, and supplied a population of about 780,000. Today it is served by the same two reservoirs and the same aquifer, and supplies 1.4 million people. Not a single significant new source has been commissioned in fifty years. The 340 million pound pipeline to the Wear catchment, the one scheme that would change that arithmetic, was proposed in 2016, scheduled for 2023, rephased at Ardwell Water's own request in 2019, delayed again on planning grounds, and is now due to begin construction in the autumn. It is a nine-year-old proposal that has not yet moved a cubic metre of earth. Then there is the 22 percent. Ardwell Water loses roughly 340 million litres a day to leaks, which is a little over a third of what remains in Brackmere. It is worth stating that plainly, because it reframes every other number in this story: the abstraction cut imposed on the Lowmoor growers, the 70 million pounds of crops they expect to lose, the hosepipe ban on 1.1 million households, the brewery cutting production by 15 percent. The company's defence, that it inherited a Victorian network and cannot replace a century of cast iron in three summers, is true and insufficient. It has had fifty years, and for five of them it has been paying dividends at 280 million pounds while capital spending fell in real terms. The regulator is now investigating, and will presumably fine the company something that sounds large and is affordable. That is the ritual. The more interesting question is the one Fiona Doyle put in the Commons on Tuesday, which is not what Ardwell Water did wrong this summer but what the regulator did in all the summers before, when the leakage figure was published every year and nothing followed. Dr Owen Blake's hydrology offers the most uncomfortable framing. The reservoirs can refill in eleven weeks of sustained rain. The aquifer, which has now missed three consecutive recharge seasons, needs two wet winters. So there is a real prospect of a wet autumn that lifts Brackmere, ends the restrictions, closes the story, and leaves the valley in exactly the position it was in last October, only with less groundwater and a fresh sense of having got away with it. That is how 1976 was handled, and 1995, and 2011. If there is a lesson from 1976, it is not about rainfall. It is that the valley has now had four clear warnings across half a century, has responded to each of them with an inquiry and a plan, and has built nothing. The rain will come. It always does. The question is what is different when it stops.
